# mindthegap {.unnumbered}

An R package for Agent Based Modelling (ABM) of whole blood donors donating at stochastic intervals.

# Overview

## Themes / Analytical methods

_R package, OOP with R6 classes, coupled ordinary differential equations for System Dynamics, Agent Based Modelling, Monte Carlo Methods,  Shiny app, composite metric, Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis_

## Business Problem

European law allows more frequent donation than NHSBT currently allows in England, so would it be a good idea to let people donate more frequently?

### Academic aim

On reducing the minimum allowed interval between successive blood donations, does any
increase in blood supply significantly outweigh any deterioration of body iron health in
donors?

## Scoping and planning

![Extract from a presentation on the project](images/mindthegap/abm_scope.png)

After interviewing clinical stakeholders, I recognised the aim of the model should be to simulate a cohort of blood donors and their instances of successful blood donations over a fixed time period. The distribution of the number of donations made by each simulated donor, and the intervals between them, should be expected to be a function of:
* The minimum interval
* The donor’s individual preferred interval between donations
* The time required for the donor’s blood iron levels to replenish sufficiently to pass the
Hb test

A reduction in the minimum interval is expected to increase the total number of donations
from donors over a fixed period of time, accompanied by an increase in the frequency and
severity of adverse effects on donors’ body iron health. The model should allow the practitioner
to vary, as an input parameter, the minimum allowed donation interval, and should
return a quantified set of donor outcomes, pertaining to blood supply and donor body iron
health.

Model methodology and outputs should be transparent, explicit, and granular enough for a practitioner to draw quantitative, parameterised insights and statistical expectations surrounding the tradeoff
between blood supply and donor body iron health. Simultaneously, model outputs should
be accessible and practical enough to lend themselves to a solving a cost-benefit analysis
rooted in that trade-off, and to reasonably inform a recommendation for an operational intervention
or policy.

## Assumptions

Key assumptions relate to:

* A sequential process flow for a donor choosing to donate blood through to the physical donation
* Distributional assumptions governing how long after their last donation a donor will choose to donate
* The dynamics of iron in the human body (especially replenishment) that govern whether a donor passes the pre-donation Haemoglobin test

## Limitations {#limitations}

The main limitation of this work is that inherent to modelling two extremely complex domains - human altruistic behaviour and biology. As such, I conducted the literature review and model design with the aim that the complexity of the project would be sufficient to capture the significant drivers and effects in the real-world system, while allowing me to write, validate, and present a model in reasonable time that was accessible, reproducible, and not over-engineered. 

## Technical choices

* I recognised the suitability of Agent-Based Modelling (ABM), given the idiosyncratic and behavioural nature of donors choosing to donate. A good model would require fine control over a range of different parameters and variables. 

::: {.panel_tabset}

### Agent Based Model overview

![Overview of ABM paradigm](images/mindthegap/abm_intro.png)

### ABM example

![Example application of ABM](images/mindthegap/abm_example_ecology.png)

### Example parameters and variables
![Extract from presentation on project](images/mindthegap/abm_example_parameters.png)
:::

* I decided to develop an R package to allow for fine control over testing different scenarios under different parameters. The donors, with their preferences, variabiality, and complex iron dynamics, warranted the use of an Object Oriented Programming approach using R6 Classes. Donor objects are instantiated, equipped with their own stochastic characteristics and behaviour, and iron replenishment mechanics.
* I used a Monte Carlo Method with hierarchical sampling to effectively and efficiently simulate a highly stochastic system of a donor's donation activity.
* I used a composite metric of a linear combination of donations and permanent deferrals (after three failed pre-donation Haemoglobin tests, donors cannot return)
* I included observables relating to "wasted slots" and donor burnout, for scope to extend the composite metric

## Validation
Model outputs from the baseline scenario (current minimum interval rules) were compared with operational data to ensure they were with a reasonable variance. The observables tested included rates of donation given attendance, rates of Hb rejections, and rates of permanent deferrals (Hb rejections on three successive attendances).

## Impact
As discussed in @results, the work allowed me to accessibly and tangibly demonstrate a finding in the literature (conducted by a different blood service), which had not been explored in the English blood service - that Hb testing alone is an insufficient marker for iron health and fitness to donate. On presenting and discussing the results with the organisation's Associate Medical Director of Donor Medicine and Plasma for Medicines, plans to implement the shorter minumum intervals were suspended.

![Coupled ordinary differential equations representing the stock and flow model for iron dynamics in the body](images/mindthegap/hb_ferritin_ivp.png)

# Output / Results {#results}

The simulations demonstrated an effect discussed in the literature, that Hb levels are not a good marker for iron health, because iron is also stored in a buffer protein, ferritin. Allowing donors to donate purely on Hb levels risks allowing donations to occur while in poor iron health. The simulations also demonstrated that donations from donors assigned at birth female are more likely to be given while in poor iron health
![While donors assigned at birth female are allowed to donate less often, a donation from a donor assigned at birth female is more likely to be given while the donor was in poor iron health, compared with one from a donor assigned at birth male.](images/mindthegap/inequalities.png)
![Donations can occur where Hb is normal, but ferritin has not fully replenished](images/mindthegap/hb_replenishment_curve.png)
![The case for ferritin testing](images/mindthegap/ferritin_testing.png)

![Raw model outputs that lend themselves to different objective functions based on organisational objectives](images/mindthegap/model_outputs.png)

# Relevance to the Senior Data Scientist role

## Packages
Packaging code allows for reproducibility and collaboration, both inside and outside the organisation. My experience in developing packages also makes we well positioned to contribute to the ICB's existing packages such as NCLRtemplates.

## Agent Based Models
As discussed in @limitations, modelling behaviour and outcomes of people in a healthcare context is complex and stochastic. People are individualistic intersections of demographics, motivations, and biology. As such, my work in ABM and Monte Carlo Methods is directly transferrable to a range of domains requiring forecasting, comparison, and evaluation of different interventions and policies.


# What I learnt/would improve
* I would extend the objective function to allow for better quantification of outcomes, for example to include the cost of healthcare for people with iron deficiency

![A more sophisticated objective function](images/mindthegap/objective_function.PNG)

* I included a parameter to adjust for different population-level normal Hb levels. I would use this to explore inequalities affecting populations of people who have lower normal levels of Hb - this is directly applicable to the observation in the organisation that Black African and Black Caribbean attendees are more likely to experience Hb rejections than other people.
